chunks.text: A slope field is a picture of a differential equation dy/dx = f(x, y), drawing the slope at each grid point as a short tangent segment.
Each segment in a slope field shows the direction a solution curve would head through that point.
A solution of the differential equation is a curve that stays tangent to the field segments at every point it passes through.
Slope fields give a qualitative understanding of solutions even when the equation cannot be solved with a formula.
To build a slope field, evaluate dy/dx = f(x, y) at each grid point and draw a short segment with that slope.
The length of a slope-field segment carries no information; only its direction (slope) matters.
A slope of 0 gives a horizontal segment, a large slope gives a steep segment, and an undefined slope gives a vertical segment.
If dy/dx depends only on x, the slope is constant along each vertical line, so every column of segments looks identical.
If dy/dx depends only on y, the slope is constant along each horizontal line, so every row of segments looks identical.
If dy/dx depends on both x and y, the slopes vary throughout the plane with no simple row or column repetition.
Example: for dy/dx = x + y, the slope at (1, 0) is 1, at (1, 1) is 2, and at (−1, 1) is 0.
For dy/dx = x + y, horizontal segments occur along the line y = −x, where x + y = 0.
A slope-field segment is a piece of the tangent line, not the solution curve; the curve does not jump from segment to segment.
Because the slope usually depends on both x and y, it must be re-evaluated at each grid point rather than assumed constant.
To sketch a particular solution, start at the given point and trace a curve that follows the segments, staying tangent to the field.
Tracing a solution is like steering with a current: always head the direction the field points at your current position.
For well-behaved equations exactly one solution passes through each point, so solution curves never cross.
To match a differential equation to a slope field, first check whether the slope depends on x only, y only, or both.
Then locate where segments are horizontal (slope zero) and vertical (undefined) and check where slopes are positive or negative.
Example: dy/dx = x has horizontal segments along the y-axis (x = 0), while dy/dx = y has horizontal segments along the x-axis (y = 0).
Slope fields require no solving yet reveal where solutions increase, decrease, level off, or blow up.
Following a slope field in small steps is the geometric idea behind Euler's method, the numerical technique for approximating solutions.
